Utility- based control was simulated through the system, but not integrated at the time of the project. 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications 1.3.3 Legacy Devices and Interoperability: Grid(Barry Mather, NLR) In this talk, Barry Mather from NLR’s Power Systems Engineering Center illustrated the pervasive nature of legacy systems in power grids by opening with a compelling historical example from Germany in 2011. At that time, Ger- many had installed 14,000 megawatts (MW) of solar PV capacity, with 70% connected to the low-voltage grid across 400,000 systems larger than 10 kW. A critical vulnerability was discovered: all solar generation would simultane- ously trip offline if grid frequency reached 50.2 hertz (Hz), potentially causing a nationwide blackout. This scenario exemplified how legacy control systems designed for simple maintenance procedures failed to anticipate the massive penetration of distributed solar resources, ultimately requiring a costly retrofit of all affected control systems. Mather emphasized that nearly everything in the electrical grid represents legacy infrastructure, from the fundamen- tal 120 Vac utilization voltage and 60 Hz frequency standards in the United States to transformer configurations and voltage regulation philosophies established decades ago. These design decisions, some made 50-100 years ago, are now "locked" into what has become the world’s largest engineered system operating on the continental scale. The presentation highlighted how these legacy choices create ongoing challenges as the grid undergoes rapid transforma- tion in generation resource mix, load characteristics, and societal expectations for reliability and performance. The core technical analysis focused on a comprehensive study of legacy distributed PV systems in the Western Interconnection, examining voltage ride-through capabilities under various fault scenarios. Using the Heavy Sum- mer 2023 planning case with high levels of utility-scale (17%) and distributed (5%) renewable sources, Mather’s team modeled three-phase fault scenarios across all Western Interconnection paths. The study revealed that under legacy Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1547-2003 standards (IEEE 2003), approximately 4,000 MW of distributed generation would be lost during fault conditions, compared to only 1,500 MW under the most advanced IEEE 1547-2018 Category III standards (IEEE 2018), demonstrating the critical importance of updat- ing legacy protection standards (Basso 2014; Kenyon and Mather 2020). During the discussion, Mather addressed questions about recent grid blackouts, noting that while the February 2021 blackouts in Texas (FERC and NERC 2021; King et al. 2021; Flores et al. 2023) may not be the best example for renewable-related issues, events in April 2025 in the Iberian Peninsula (Lauby 2025; Lara et al. 2025) likely involved both renewable and conventional generation controls contributing to system instability. He emphasized that blackouts typically result from configuration and programming issues rather than the inherent capabilities of energy resources themselves.
